newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Grenade explodes at UN flat in Bosnian Serb region.
newsitem.headline: Grenade explodes at UN flat in Bosnian Serb region.

text.p: A hand grenade shattered windows in the apartment of an international police officer early on Friday in the latest Bosnian Serb retaliatory attack over a NATO swoop on indicted war criminals.
U.N. spokesman Alun Roberts said the sleeping officer was not injured in the explosion in Bosanska Gradiska, about 50 km (30 miles) north of Banja Luka, in Bosnia's Serb entity.
"There was quite a bit of damage to the balcony and living room windows," Roberts told Reuters.

The blast was the fifth in as many days targeting peacekeepers or civilian international officials involved in the effort to rebuild Bosnia after war. In a sixth incident, a U.S. soldier was slightly hurt in an attack with a sickle.
The NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force said another explosion was heard in Prijedor, southwest of Banja Luka, overnight but there were no other details available.
Roberts said the wave of minor explosions "appear to be a form of low-level intimidation" in retaliation for the NATO arrest operation last week.
There was no plan to evacuate U.N. staff members, he said. "We will take common sense precautionary measures but our work will continue as usual."

Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders were outraged by NATO's pounce on two Serbs charged with war crimes by a U.N. tribunal. One was seized and extradited, the other was shot dead when he resisted British soldiers trying to arrest him.
The U.N.-affiliated International Police Task Force had not observed any change in the public mood towards IPTF in any of its police stations throughout Serb entity, Roberts said.
Western officials confirmed that ordinary Serbs showed little enthusiasm for taking up arms against well-armed NATO troops and were preoccupied with daily survival in a collapsing economy.

Suspicions as to who is behind the bombings have focused on elements of the nationalist ruling party and police loyal to former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, a fugitive indicted war criminal who has tried to obstruct the implementation of Bosnia's 1995 peace treaty.

A few protests against the NATO action have failed to produce big crowds but recent rallies against pro-Karadzic leadership attracted thousands of people in support of postwar Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.

She has led a campaign against rampant corruption in Serb territory, accusing Karadzic and his allies of profiting off "shameful" smuggling deals while the rest of the population languishes in abject poverty and cut off from Western aid.

The suspect shot dead in the NATO raid, Simo Drljaca, was a powerful figure in the Prijedor region and loyal ally of Karadzic. He was charged with orchestrating ethnic expulsions of Moslems and Croats early in the Bosnian war in 1992.
Human rights workers say Drljaca and his associates enriched themselves off property seized from non-Serbs and kept strict control of international aid donated to Prijedor.
Karadzic has been indicted twice by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague but has dismissed the charges.

Roberts said posters bearing Karadzic's photograph had been plastered on U.N. offices and other international agencies in Serb territory. Below Karadzic's picture were the words: "Don't touch him - he means peace".
Asked about the Karadzic posters, NATO spokesman Major Michael Wright said: "I would rather have seen his face appear in The Hague then in downtown Banja Luka".
